This article is for the person who sets up atima for a lab, a department or
the public: one server that many people use from their browsers, each
signed in to their own account. It walks through the container setup that
is kept in the `deploy/` folder of the
[repository](https://github.com/cmmr/atima): the atima server, a reverse
proxy (Caddy) in front of it for HTTPS and rate limits, and a nightly
backup. To use atima alone on your own computer you need none of this; see
[Using atima on your own computer](local-install.html).

Everything here was built and run on one development machine with Docker
Desktop. It has not yet been run on a public server, with a real
certificate, or with a real sign-in provider.


## What you need

- A Linux machine with [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/)
  and its Compose plugin. Four CPU cores and 8 GB of memory are a
  reasonable start; see [How large a server](#how-large-a-server).
- A host name for the server (for example `atima.example.org`) that points
  at the machine, with ports 80 and 443 reachable from the internet, so
  that Caddy can get a certificate from Let's Encrypt. If your institution
  puts its own proxy in front, see
  [Behind another proxy](#behind-another-proxy).
- A registration with a sign-in provider: a client id and a client secret.
  [Setting up sign-in](sign-in.html) explains how to get them from Globus
  Auth or ORCID. You can start without them and try the server as a guest.
- Disk space for the data: the database is small; each uploaded dataset is
  stored once, as a file of at most the upload limit (50 MB by default).
  Backups should go to a different disk.


## The pieces

`deploy/compose.yaml` starts three containers:

| Container | What it does |
|---|---|
| `atima`  | The atima server: one R process that answers requests and owns the database, and its worker processes, which do the computing. Runs as an unprivileged user on a read-only file system. Listens on port 8080 inside the Docker network only. |
| `caddy`  | [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com) with the rate-limit module. Gets and renews the TLS certificate, passes requests on to atima, tells atima the truth about each request (HTTPS or not, the visitor's address), and limits how often one address may call the expensive routes. |
| `backup` | The same image as `atima`, running a loop that makes a backup every night. |

and keeps data in Docker volumes:

| Volume | Mounted at | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `atima_data` | `/var/lib/atima` | The database (`sqlite.db`), the stored data files (`files/`), and a cache that can be deleted at any time (`cache/`). **This is what must not be lost.** |
| `atima_temp` | `/var/tmp/atima` | Figures and exports waiting to be downloaded. The server deletes them after a day. |
| `atima_backup` | `/backup` | The backups, unless you point `ATIMA_BACKUP_DIR` somewhere better. |
| `caddy_data`, `caddy_config` | | Caddy's certificates and state. |

Every setting is an environment variable. They are read from the file
`deploy/.env`, which you make from `deploy/.env.example` and which is not
in git. No file in the repository needs editing, and no secret belongs in
one.


## A trial run on your own machine

This starts the whole stack on `http://localhost`, without a certificate
and without a sign-in provider. You can use it as a guest.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/cmmr/atima.git
cd atima/deploy
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build
```

The first build downloads R and about 150 packages and takes ten to
fifteen minutes; the image is about 2.7 GB. Later builds reuse most of it.
When the command returns, check that the three containers are up and that
`atima` is "healthy":

```sh
docker compose ps
```

Then open <http://localhost>. The two example projects are there, and you
can upload a file. "Sign in" will not work yet: the example `.env` has a
placeholder where the client id and secret go.

To try signing in before you have registered with a provider, the
repository has a mock provider that signs anyone in under any name they
type. It is for a test on your own machine only:

```sh
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f ../loadtest/compose.mock.yaml up -d
```

To stop the trial and delete its data:

```sh
docker compose down --volumes
```


## Setting up the real server

Edit `deploy/.env`. The settings that every server needs:

```sh
ATIMA_SITE_ADDRESS=atima.example.org
ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL=https://atima.example.org
ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=<client id from the provider>
ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<client secret from the provider>
ATIMA_OPERATOR=the Example Lab at Example University
ATIMA_CONTACT=atima@example.org
ATIMA_BACKUP_DIR=/mnt/backup/atima
```

- `ATIMA_SITE_ADDRESS` is what Caddy serves. A bare host name means HTTPS
  with a certificate from Let's Encrypt.
- `ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL` is the address people type. The sign-in provider sends
  people back to `<ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL>/auth/callback`, and that exact address
  is what you register with the provider.
- `ATIMA_OPERATOR` and `ATIMA_CONTACT` are shown on the app's "Privacy and
  terms" page: who runs this server, and an email address or web page for
  questions.
- `ATIMA_BACKUP_DIR` is a directory on the host for the backups, on a
  different disk from the data or on a network share. It must be writable
  by user id 10001, the user the containers run as:
  `sudo chown 10001 /mnt/backup/atima`.

Keep `.env` readable by you alone (`chmod 600 .env`): it holds the client
secret. If you use Docker secrets or another secret store instead, give the
`atima` container `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE`, the path of a file that
holds the secret, in place of `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET`.

Then start it:

```sh
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs -f atima
```

Once the site works over HTTPS, add `ATIMA_HSTS=max-age=31536000` to `.env`
and run `docker compose up -d` again. Browsers that have visited will then
refuse to use the site without HTTPS for a year.

### All settings

The settings of `atima::run()` are described in its help page; each is the
environment variable `ATIMA_<NAME>`. `deploy/compose.yaml` passes these on
from `.env`:

| In `.env` | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ATIMA_SITE_ADDRESS` | | What Caddy serves: a host name (HTTPS), `http://localhost` (trial), or `:80` (behind another proxy). |
| `ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL` | | The address people type, with `https://` and no path. |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_ISSUER` | `https://auth.globus.org` | The sign-in provider. |
| `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_ID`, `ATIMA_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | | From the provider. |
| `ATIMA_ADMINS` | none | Administrators, by the provider's identifier for them, separated by commas. |
| `ATIMA_OPERATOR`, `ATIMA_CONTACT` | none | Shown on the "Privacy and terms" page. |
| `ATIMA_WORKERS` | half the cores, at most 4 | Worker processes. |
| `ATIMA_MAX_CPUS` | cores divided by workers | CPU cores one job may use. |
| `ATIMA_TIME_LIMIT` | 60 | Seconds a job may run. |
| `ATIMA_JOBS_PER_USER` | 16 | Jobs one account may have waiting or running. |
| `ATIMA_MAX_UPLOAD_MB` | 50 | Largest upload. Caddy enforces the same number. |
| `ATIMA_CACHE_SIZE_MB` | 100 | Size of the cache of computed results. |
| `ATIMA_SESSION_HOURS`, `ATIMA_GUEST_DAYS`, `ATIMA_SIGNIN_DAYS` | 24, 30, 30 | How long an idle tab, a guest and a sign-in last. |
| `ATIMA_TRUSTED_PROXIES` | none | Only [behind another proxy](#behind-another-proxy). |
| `ATIMA_HSTS` | off | `max-age=31536000` once HTTPS works. |
| `ATIMA_HTTP_PORT`, `ATIMA_HTTPS_PORT` | 80, 443 | The host's ports for Caddy. |
| `ATIMA_BACKUP_DIR` | a Docker volume | Where backups go. |
| `ATIMA_BACKUP_HOUR`, `ATIMA_BACKUP_DAILY`, `ATIMA_BACKUP_WEEKLY`, `ATIMA_BACKUP_UPGRADES` | 8, 7, 4, 3 | See [Backups](#backups). |
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_...` | | See [Rate limits](#rate-limits). |


## Administrators and the public projects

An administrator can edit and unpublish any public project and arranges the
public list: on the Projects page, administrators see controls to create,
rename, move and delete the collections (folders) that public projects are
listed under, and to move public projects between them. Administrators
cannot open other people's private projects.

To make someone an administrator, have them sign in once, then find the
provider's identifier for them:

```sh
docker compose exec atima Rscript -e 'con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "/var/lib/atima/sqlite.db"); print(DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT full_name, sub FROM users WHERE is_guest = 0"))'
```

Put the `sub` values, separated by commas, in `ATIMA_ADMINS` in `.env`, run
`docker compose up -d`, and have them sign in again. From then on
`ATIMA_ADMINS` decides who is an administrator, at every sign-in.

A new server shows two example projects from rbiom. Anyone who is signed in
and can edit a project can publish it, under a short name of their
choosing, and public projects are not reviewed before they appear; the
"Privacy and terms" page says so. To add example datasets of your own,
sign in, upload them, and publish them.


## What Caddy does, and why

The configuration is `deploy/caddy/Caddyfile`. You should not need to
change it, but if you use a different proxy, this is the list to reproduce.

- **Passes everything on.** `/api/` (the app's requests), `/auth/` (the
  way to and from the sign-in provider), `/www/` (the app's own files),
  `/tmp/` (figures and exports), `/mcp` (for AI apps; not offered by shared
  servers yet), and the pages and downloads at `/<project key>` and
  `/<project key>/<file>`.
- **Says whether the visitor used HTTPS, and from which address.** Caddy
  sets `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Host` and
  `X-Real-IP` itself on every request and discards what the visitor sent
  under those names. atima is told to believe `X-Forwarded-Proto`
  (`ATIMA_FORWARDED_PROTO_HEADER`, set in `compose.yaml`). A proxy that
  passed a visitor's own `X-Forwarded-Proto` through would let them switch
  off the cookie's `Secure` flag for their own session.
- **Does not cache.** atima sends its own files with
  `Cache-Control: no-cache`, so that browsers ask before reusing a script
  and never run old scripts against an upgraded server. A proxy may answer
  those "has it changed?" requests, but must not keep `/www` files longer
  than that.
- **Does not buffer or compress `/mcp`.** Answers there are passed on the
  moment they are ready.
- **Refuses uploads over the limit** before they reach atima.
- **Limits rates** (below).
- **Writes no access log.** Request paths contain the keys that give access
  to private projects (`/<key>`), so a proxy's access log would hold them.
  atima's own log records each request by its route, without the key.

The page atima serves sets a Content-Security-Policy that allows nothing
from other sites, and loads nothing from other sites. If your proxy adds a
policy of its own, both apply: check that figures, fonts and the CSV
download of a statistics table still work.

### Rate limits

Limits are per visitor address and per minute. They protect the routes
that cost the server something before any account is involved. Inside
atima, each account is also limited to `ATIMA_JOBS_PER_USER` jobs waiting
or running at once; a request over that gets status 429 and a message to
wait.

| Setting | Default | Applies to | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_SESSION_INIT` | 120 | `POST /api/session/init` | Each call from a new browser makes a guest account. |
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_SIGNIN` | 30 | `/auth/` | Each sign-in is remembered for ten minutes and calls the provider. |
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_LEGACY` | 10 | `POST /api/legacy/list`, `/api/legacy/start` | Checking an old password takes a worker about a second. |
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_DOWNLOADS` | 60 | `GET /<key>/<file>` | Needs no session, so anyone with a key can queue work. |
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_OAUTH` | 30 | `/oauth/`, `/.well-known/` | For AI apps signing in, in a later version. |
| `ATIMA_LIMIT_API` | 1200 | `/api/` as a whole | A ceiling. |

A lecture room of people may share one address, so the defaults are
generous. If a class is turned away with status 429 when everyone opens the
page together, raise `ATIMA_LIMIT_SESSION_INIT`.

### Behind another proxy

If your institution's proxy or load balancer terminates TLS and passes
requests to this machine, keep Caddy, on plain HTTP, for the rate limits
and the header rules:

```sh
ATIMA_SITE_ADDRESS=:80
ATIMA_PUBLIC_URL=https://atima.example.org
ATIMA_TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.0.0.5/32
```

`ATIMA_TRUSTED_PROXIES` is the address (or network, in CIDR form; several
are separated by spaces) that the institution's proxy connects from. Caddy
then believes that proxy's `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and
nobody else's. The proxy in front must set those two headers itself on
every request, overwriting what the visitor sent, must pass the `Host`
header through, must allow request bodies up to the upload limit, and must
not cache.

### Without containers, or with another proxy

atima is an R package and the server is one function, so it can run
without Docker: install the package, set the same `ATIMA_` variables, and
run `atima::run()` under a service manager that restarts it and stops it
with an interrupt signal (SIGINT), which is what makes it shut down
cleanly. Put a reverse proxy in front that does what the list above says.
`deploy/Dockerfile` lists the system libraries and the optional R packages
a full server needs. Only the Caddy configuration in this repository has
been tested.

A server with `auth = "none"` cannot be put behind a proxy: it refuses to
listen on anything but the loopback address and refuses requests addressed
to any other host name. That is deliberate. A server that other computers
can reach needs accounts.


## Looking after the server

### Logs

```sh
docker compose logs -f atima
```

atima writes one line of JSON per request (`"event":"request"`: method,
route, status, milliseconds, user id) and per error, to the container's
standard error. An error shown to a person carries a short id; the log
line with the same `id` has the details. Requests are logged by route, so
project keys and what requests contain are not in the log; error details
can include values from the failed request. Other events worth knowing:

| Event | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sign_in`, `sign_out` | Someone signed in or out. |
| `oidc_discovery_failed` | The sign-in provider could not be reached at start-up. The server runs and tries again at the first sign-in. |
| `job_timeout` | A job passed the time limit and was stopped. |
| `worker_killed`, `worker_lost` | A worker process had to be ended, or died; a new one took its place. |
| `cleanup` | Old sessions, guests, drafts or files were deleted. |
| `db_backup`, `db_migration` | A schema upgrade (see below). |
| `legacy_import_failed` | A project could not be imported from an older atima. |
| `unhealthy` | The health check failed. |

Docker keeps container logs without limit unless told otherwise; set up
[log rotation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/logging/configure/) for the
Docker daemon.

### Health

`GET /api/health` answers `{"status":"ok"}` with status 200 when the
database answers and the worker pool is running, and 503 otherwise. It
starts no session. The image's own health check calls it every 30 seconds,
and `docker compose ps` shows the result.

### Stopping and restarting

```sh
docker compose stop        # or: docker compose restart atima
```

Stopping interrupts the R process. atima then cancels running jobs (people
see "The server is shutting down"), stops its worker processes, writes the
database's pending changes into `sqlite.db` and exits with status 0, within
a few seconds; Docker waits up to 30. Imports from an older atima that
were running end, and can be started again.

### Upgrading

```sh
git pull
docker compose up -d --build
```

When a new version needs a different database structure, the server first
saves a copy of the database as `sqlite.db.v<N>.<date>.bak` in the data
volume, then upgrades the database in place; the log shows `db_backup` and
one `db_migration` line per step. To go back to the older version, stop
the server, restore the last backup from before the upgrade (below), and
start the older image. The backup service keeps the three newest of these
upgrade copies.

### Backups

The `backup` container makes a backup every night at `ATIMA_BACKUP_HOUR`
(UTC, default 8). A backup is a consistent copy of the database, made with
SQLite's backup interface while the server runs, plus the stored data
files, each of which is copied once because they never change. Copying
`sqlite.db` by hand while the server runs is not a backup: the database
uses a write-ahead log, and the file alone can be incomplete.

The newest `ATIMA_BACKUP_DAILY` (7) backups are kept, and the newest of
each of the last `ATIMA_BACKUP_WEEKLY` (4) weeks. Backups hold everything
the server holds, including data that people have since deleted, until the
backup itself is removed. Protect the backup directory as you protect the
server.

```sh
docker compose run --rm backup backups     # list the backups
docker compose run --rm backup backup      # make one now
```

To restore, stop the server first:

```sh
docker compose stop atima
docker compose run --rm backup restore atima-20270115T080000Z.db
docker compose start atima
```

The database that was there is kept beside the restored one as
`sqlite.db.before-restore.<date>`; delete it when you are sure. If the
server was not shut down cleanly, `restore` refuses, because it cannot
tell a crashed server from a running one; add the word `force` after the
backup's name once you are sure the server is stopped.

Test a restore on another machine before you rely on the backups.

### Importing from an older atima

[Importing from an older atima](legacy-import.html) explains how to make
the file that holds an old installation's data. To give it to the
container, set in `.env`

```sh
ATIMA_LEGACY_FILE=/srv/atima/atima2.sqlite
ATIMA_LEGACY_LABEL=atima.example.org before 2027
```

and add the second compose file to every command:

```sh
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.legacy.yaml up -d
```

The file is mounted read-only. It is as sensitive as the old database:
keep it readable only by user id 10001 (`chown 10001`, `chmod 400`). An
import can keep a worker busy for up to 15 minutes per project, so run at
least two workers while people are importing.


## How large a server

Memory: each worker is an R process with rbiom loaded. On the development
machine a worker held 500 to 650 MB after drawing plots of the larger
example project (1,006 samples), and the main process 400 MB. Allow 1 GB
per worker, plus 1 GB for the main process and Caddy; datasets near the
upload limit will need more. CPU: `ATIMA_WORKERS` times
`ATIMA_MAX_CPUS` should not exceed the cores the container may use. atima
reads the container's CPU limit, so its defaults (half the cores as
workers, at most four) follow a limit you set with Docker.

What happens when the server is too small: requests that need a worker
wait in a queue of ten per worker. A plot that would take one second takes
longer because it waits; when the queue is full, new requests are answered
503 ("The server is busy") until there is room. Requests that need no
worker (loading the page, the project list, signing in) are answered by
the main process and stay fast.

The repository has a load test (`loadtest/`) that simulates people
browsing, one person starting many jobs at once, and many people signing
in together. `loadtest/README.md` has the measurements from the
development machine and says how to run the test against your own server
before you open it.


## What is not protected

- Anyone who has a project's link (its private key) can open the project
  and download its data. That is how sharing by link works; "New link" on
  the Sharing page replaces the key.
- Links to figures and exports work for anyone who has them, for a day.
- Whoever administers the machine can read everything on it. The data is
  not encrypted at rest.
- Public projects are published by their editors without review.
